findings.claim: The Nicene Creed "is recited at every Catholic Mass" (repeated in the glossary definition and a flashcard).
findings.truth: The Creed is said at Mass on Sundays and solemnities, not at every Mass.
findings.evidence: General Instruction of the Roman Missal 68

findings.claim: The Creed "declares 'We believe in one God'".
findings.truth: The English text said at Mass since Advent 2011 begins "I believe in one God". "We believe" is the withdrawn 1973 translation.
findings.evidence: Roman Missal third edition (ICEL 2011), in use in England and Wales since Advent 2011

findings.claim: "The Arian heresy (condemned at Nicaea) held that the Son was a lesser, created being (homoiousios - similar substance)."
findings.truth: Arius held that the Son was created and not of the Father's substance. Homoiousios ('of similar substance') was the semi-Arian compromise word of the 350s, after Nicaea, not the Arian position condemned in 325.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Arianism; Homoousion

findings.truth: The specification names four places of pilgrimage: Jerusalem, Lourdes, Rome and Walsingham (1A 2.6). Naming only two leaves a student unprepared for a question on Rome or Jerusalem.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/religious-studies-a-1RA0.md 1A 2.6

findings.claim: "examiners consistently note the alternative view is the weakest part of student responses".
findings.truth: An invented examiner claim. The teachable fact is that an answer that argues only one side cannot reach the top band.
findings.evidence: no source; house rule against invented examiner claims

findings.claim: A 5-mark model answer gives "Source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1210 (seven sacraments, including the Eucharist as a real presence of Christ)" as the source for transubstantiation.
findings.truth: Catechism 1210-1211 lists and groups the seven sacraments; it says nothing about the real presence. The specification cites 1210-1211 for the sacraments only.
findings.evidence: vatican.va, Catechism 1210-1211; specs/edexcel/religious-studies-a-1RA0.md 1A 2.1

findings.claim: Lourdes: "Over six million visitors a year."
findings.truth: Sources disagree. Wikipedia's article on the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes gives "around four million tourists coming every year"; the sanctuary's own older figure is about six million. No single true value was found and no mark depends on the number, so the text is left alone.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes

findings.claim: The lesson cites "Lumen Gentium (1964)" for "source and summit of the Christian life" and tells students to learn the document name and the year.
findings.truth: The phrase stands at Lumen Gentium 11 ("the Eucharistic sacrifice, which is the fount and apex of the whole Christian life"), but the specification cites Lumen Gentium paragraph 7 for it. Options: (a) leave the lesson as it is, naming the document and year only - safe under either reading; (b) add "paragraph 7" to match the specification; (c) add "paragraph 11" to match the document. Recommend (a), no edit.
findings.evidence: vatican.va, Lumen Gentium 11; specs/edexcel/religious-studies-a-1RA0.md 1A 2.2
findings.ruling: Leave: no paragraph named; naming either risks a mismatch.

findings.claim: "The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2501 states that sacred art is 'true and beautiful' when it 'corresponds to its specific purpose: evoking and glorifying, in faith and adoration, the transcendent mystery of God.'" The same number is repeated in the conclusion, the exam tip, a model answer and a flashcard.
findings.truth: That sentence is Catechism 2502, and it reads "Sacred art is true and beautiful when its form corresponds to its particular vocation: evoking and glorifying, in faith and adoration, the transcendent mystery of God." Catechism 2501 is about man expressing his relationship with God the Creator through the beauty of his art.
findings.evidence: vatican.va, Catechism 2501-2503

summary: Six lessons checked; every lesson carries at least one finding. The doctrinal content is sound, but the Nicene Creed is quoted throughout from the withdrawn 1973 translation, the sacred-art sentence is attributed to Catechism 2501 instead of 2502, Matthew 5:17 and Catechism 1030 are misquoted, and every lesson sets a 3-mark Describe question and a 12-mark 'Discuss' question, neither of which exists on this paper. One ADJUDICATE: the specification cites Lumen Gentium paragraph 7 for 'source and summit', which actually stands at Lumen Gentium 11.
